# Overview {.unnumbered}
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Preface

On the real projective plane, a line $\ell$ and a conic $\mathcal{C}$ may meet at $0,1,2$ points. However, we may always study the involution on $\ell$ induced by $\mathcal{C}$ (if they are not tangent)
$$
\varphi:\ell\to \ell,\, P\mapsto \ell\cap \mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(P)
$$
where $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(P)$ is the polar of $P$ with respect to $\mathcal{C}$.

If $\mathcal{C}$ and $\ell$ intersect at two points $X,Y$, then $\varphi(X)=X,\varphi(Y)=Y$. This shows that if two conics $\mathcal{C}_1,\mathcal{C}_2$ induces the same involution on $\ell$, then the intersections of $\mathcal{C}_1,\ell$ and $\mathcal{C}_2,\ell$ are the same (if $\mathcal{C}_i$ and $\ell$ intersect at two points). In other words, to find the intersection of a line and a conic, it suffices to study the induced involution of the conic on the line.

Consider the involution $\varphi$ on the line of infinity $\ell_\infty$ induced by a circle $\omega$. If $\infty_1\in\ell_\infty$, then $\varphi(\infty_1)$ is the point of infinity of the direction perpendicular to $\infty_1$. We see that $\varphi$ does not depend on the choice of $\omega$, i.e. all circles induces the same involution on $\ell_\infty$. This suggests that in a broad sense, the "intersections" of all circles and $\ell_\infty$ are the same. If we add a hypothesis that conics and lines always meet at two points (or tangent), then all circles pass through two fixed points $\infty_+,\infty_-$ on the line of infinity.

In the complex projective plane, the hypothesis is satisfied, and we call the points $\infty_\pm$ the circular points of infinity. The circumcircle $\omega$ of a triangle $ABC$ is the conic passing through $A,B,C,\infty_+,\infty_-$, and if $O$ is the center of $\omega$, then $O\infty_+,O\infty_-$ are tangent to $\omega$ (since the polar of $O$ with respect to $\omega$ is $\ell_\infty$). Besides circles, we may define angles, radical centers, and even the foci of conics projectively with the circular points of infinity. In the following, we equip a projective plane with a complex-valued cross ratio, and derive familiar geometric properties from its fundamental properties.
